newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's opposition tables no-confidence motion.
newsitem.headline: Romania's opposition tables no-confidence motion.

text.p: Romania's leftist opposition issued the text of a no-confidence motion in the centrist government on Thursday over what it called its inability to rule the country and control "economic chaos".

The motion, put forward by the former ruling Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) attacked the cabinet headed by Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea over the "imminence of a serious economic and social crisis due to the government's incompetence and adventurous actions."
Analysts said the motion was unlikely to unseat Ciorbea's government because his ruling coalition had a majority in parliament.

The motion attacked moves by the government to seek parliamentary backing for its commitment to tough economic reform, a move amounting to a vote of confidence in the six-month old administration which replaced the PDSR.
"These are clear attempts by the government to attack parliament's prerogatives and subordinate it," the motion said.
The motion said the government's reform measures had pushed Romanians' living standards to dramatic lows without providing social protection to the nation of 23 million.

"If the government assumes responsibility instead of parliament, the latter should be shut down as is not the government's lower chamber. The government cannot pass laws and also enforce them in a state of law," PDSR vice-president Adrian Nastase said recently.

In February, Ciorbea's cabinet launched a package of tough reforms, also endorsed by international lenders, aiming to slash inflation, cut the current account deficit and increase foreign exchange reserves. Restructuring or closing down loss-making companies are also part of the tough package to put the economy back on track.
The shock-therapy brought about higher prices and falling living standards for many Romanians especially after the cabinet liberalised prices and cut subsidies to all sectors.
So far, opinion polls show Romanians are determined to embrace reforms.
The motion will be read during separate sessions of the two-house parliament by next week, parliament sources said.
The PDSR, which inherited power from communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu after the 1989 revolution, was ousted in last November's elections.
Earlier this month, Romania was promised credits worth $625 million from the World Bank, which praised the Ciorbea government for its progress in introducing reforms.
The credits followed a standby loan from the International Monetary Fund, worth $430 million intended to boost the economic reform.
